- basic (single set of nodes, single set of links)
- bipartite (usually called twomode, two modes (sets/types of nodes), each link has an endnode in each mode)

   - time slices (slice = ordinary network in selected time interval)
   - sequence of events transforming the current version of network (for example a trace of the network growth or data sets from https://eventdata.parusanalytics.com/data.html , etc.)
   - description of node/link activity as temporal quantity https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13278-016-0330-4
- collection of networks

In a previous version of the guidelines, GRAND was described as "agnostic" with regard to terminology. However, the issue of terminology inevitably arises when providing a set of minimum recommendations. In the case of "edges," for example, we find the use of several synonyms, such as "ties," "arcs," "links," "connections," or "relationships," among others. It may therefore be useful to include some of these synonyms for the terms used, either in the notes or in a final section of the guidelines.

A related issue in guidelines for reporting relational data concerns the terminology employed. The incorporation of statistical physicists through network science has led to the introduction of new terms for concepts that were already used in social network analysis. Some degree of standardization could be helpful, as different names are currently used for the same indicators or network properties.

This also relates to language use. For example, in Spanish there are different terms referring to the same concept: structural holes are called “agujeros estructurales” in Spain and “hoyos estructurales” in Mexico. Greater standardization in terminology could help avoid ambiguities.

For many researchers in the social sciences, the multimode framework is significantly more intuitive. Introducing hypergraphs as a co-equal standard may cause unnecessary confusion, as the mathematical "set" logic can feel quite abstract in a social research context. By keeping hypergraphs as an optional, secondary extension, we can provide a pathway for advanced computational modeling without creating a barrier to entry for the broader community.
